speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To help assess the newborn's increasing yellow discoloration, I need to know when the jaundice first appeared and how old the baby is in hours or days. Please also let me know if the baby is feeding well and having normal wet diapers.

speaker: Patient
text: 2-week-old female newborn. The patient has been experiencing increasing yellow discoloration of her eyes and skin for 2 days. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation, initially weighed 3066 g and now weighs 3200 g. The patient is exclusively breastfed.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has the mother noticed any changes in the color of the baby's stools, such as pale or clay-colored stools, or dark urine? REQUEST TEST: Total and Direct Bilirubin

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Born at 39 weeks' gestation. Exclusive breastfeeding. Family history notable for older brother's death possibly related to liver issues. Social history: Not applicable for age.

speaker: Patient
text: Temperature of 37.1°C, pulse of 145/min, and respirations of 40/min. No other symptoms reported by the caregiver. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Acute appendicitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That previous diagnosis of acute appendicitis is highly improbable for a 2-week-old infant with jaundice, so I will disregard it. I need to confirm the bilirubin levels to determine if this is physiological jaundice or a pathological condition like biliary atresia. REQUEST TEST: Total and Direct Bilirubin

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Total Bilirubin: 16.1 mg/dL, Direct Bilirubin: 0.7 mg/dL

speaker: Doctor
text: The bilirubin results show predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which is common in breastfed infants but warrants checking for underlying hemolysis. I need to know if there is any family history of jaundice or hemolytic anemia, and whether the baby's blood type differs from the mother's. REQUEST TEST: Blood Type and Coombs Test

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal Coombs test and blood types rule out immune-mediated hemolysis, suggesting this is likely breast milk jaundice given the timing and exclusive breastfeeding. To be thorough, I will check for other causes of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia such as thyroid dysfunction or G6PD deficiency. REQUEST TEST: TSH, G6PD assay

speaker: Doctor
text: With normal thyroid and G6PD results, the diagnosis of breast milk jaundice is highly likely given the exclusive breastfeeding and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. DIAGNOSIS READY: Breast milk jaundice
